subject: Genetics
topic: Huntington Disease CAG Expansion & Histone Deacetylation Repression
stem: A 41-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of progressive involuntary, irregular, jerky, purposeless movements of his hands and face, accompanied by mood lability, severe depression, and executive cognitive decline. His father developed similar involuntary movements in his early 40s and died in a nursing facility. Physical examination demonstrates continuous rapid, non-stereotyped, involuntary movements of the upper extremities (chorea) and an inability to maintain sustained tongue protrusion ('serpentine' tongue or motor impersistence). Brain MRI reveals profound, symmetrical atrophy of the caudate nuclei and putamen with compensatory enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles. Genetic analysis identifies an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (46 repeats) in exon 1 of the HTT gene on chromosome 4p16.3. Which of the following epigenetic mechanisms directly contributes to transcriptional gene silencing and neuronal death in this patient's striatal medium spiny neurons?

options.text: Demethylation of cytosine-guanine (CpG) islands within striatal promoter regions, inducing excessive RNA polymerase II transcription
options.explanation: DNA hypomethylation typically enhances gene expression; Huntington disease is characterized by transcriptional repression driven by histone deacetylation.

options.text: Constitutive hyperacetylation of core histone H3 tails by histone deacetylase inhibitors, causing nucleosomal unfolding
options.explanation: Hyperacetylation opens chromatin and promotes transcription (the mechanism of HDAC inhibitor drugs), whereas mutant huntingtin causes hypoacetylation and silencing.

options.text: Inactivating point mutation in the DNA methyltransferase-1 (DNMT1) enzyme, preventing maintenance of genomic imprinting
options.explanation: DNMT1 maintains DNA methylation; Huntington disease is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, not DNMT1 mutations.

options.text: Selective methylation of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me3) activating downstream pro-apoptotic caspase transcription
options.explanation: H3K4me3 is an epigenetic mark of active transcription; mutant huntingtin primarily drives transcriptional silencing through loss of histone acetylation.

options.text: Mutant huntingtin binds and inactivates histone acetyltransferases (such as CBP/p300), shifting the epigenetic equilibrium toward excessive histone deacetylation and condensed, transcriptionally repressed heterochromatin
options.explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene, encoding an elongated polyglutamine tract. The mutant huntingtin protein misfolds and forms toxic intranuclear aggregates that physically bind and sequester CREB-binding protein (CBP), an essential histone acetyltransferase (HAT). Loss of HAT activity allows histone deacetylases (HDACs) to dominate, removing acetyl groups from lysine residues on histones H3 and H4. Histones become positively charged, binding tightly to negatively charged DNA to form condensed heterochromatin, silencing transcription of critical neurotrophic factors (such as BDNF) and causing selective apoptosis of striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurons.

explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene, encoding an elongated polyglutamine tract. The mutant huntingtin protein misfolds and forms toxic intranuclear aggregates that physically bind and sequester CREB-binding protein (CBP), an essential histone acetyltransferase (HAT). Loss of HAT activity allows histone deacetylases (HDACs) to dominate, removing acetyl groups from lysine residues on histones H3 and H4. Histones become positively charged, binding tightly to negatively charged DNA to form condensed heterochromatin, silencing transcription of critical neurotrophic factors (such as BDNF) and causing selective apoptosis of striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurons.
